title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing window sums from scratch versus sorting once and sliding a window with an O(1) running-sum cost formula.

sections.title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element

content.title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an integer array nums and an integer k, you may perform at most k operations, each incrementing a single element by 1 (any element, any number of times, in any order). Return the maximum possible frequency of any element after performing these operations.

blocks.caption: Sort first, then grow/shrink a window by the cost of raising every element to the window's max

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An integer array nums, and an integer k (the maximum number of +1 operations allowed, spent anywhere)"],["Output","The highest achievable frequency of any single value after spending at most k operations"],["Goal","Find this without simulating every possible way to spend the k operations"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 10^5; 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5; 1 <= k <= 10^5"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Only increments are allowed, never decrements","The cheapest way to make several numbers equal is always to raise them all up to the LARGEST among them"],["Looking for the largest group makeable within a total operation budget","Sort first, then a variable-size sliding window, since equal values after raising must have started as a contiguous sorted stretch"],["The window's \"cost\" changes non-trivially as it grows or shrinks","Maintain a running sum of the window so cost can be computed in O(1) per step, rather than resumming from scratch"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, using at most k total +1 operations (spent freely across any elements), find the highest achievable frequency of any single value.

blocks.title: Analogy: Topping Up Coins to Match the Tallest Stack
blocks.text: Like having several stacks of coins of different heights and a limited number of extra coins to add. To make the most stacks the same height, sort the stacks and pick a contiguous run, topping every shorter stack in that run up to the tallest one in it; that always costs less than raising to any taller target outside the run.

blocks.caption: Sort the values; raising a contiguous stretch up to its own largest member is always the cheapest way to equalize it

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1, 2, 4], k = 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Sorted: [1, 2, 4]. Raise 1 and 2 up to 4: costs (4-1)+(4-2) = 5","A group of 3 fours, using exactly the full budget of k=5","This uses exactly k=5 operations to make all 3 elements equal to 4"],["Answer","3","All 3 elements can be made equal using exactly the allowed budget"]]}

blocks.text: Example: nums = [1, 4, 8, 13], k = 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Sorted: [1, 4, 8, 13]. Raise 1 up to 4: costs 3 (within budget); trying to also include 8 would cost (8-4)+(8-1) = 11, over budget","A group of 2 (values 1 and 4, both raised to 4)","No group of 3 or more sorted-adjacent elements fits within the budget of k=5"],["Answer","2","This is the largest group achievable within the operation budget"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: k is very large (larger than needed to equalize everything)
When k is at least as large as the cost of raising every element up to the maximum value in nums, the entire array can be made equal, so the answer is simply nums.length.
5. How Should We Think?
Before trying every possible group of elements to equalize, notice that only incrementing is allowed, which fixes exactly how a group should be chosen and priced.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since only +1 operations are allowed, equalizing any group of numbers is always cheapest by raising every member up to the group's own largest value, never higher.

Observation 2: A group being raised to a common value doesn't need to be made of physically adjacent array elements, but after sorting, the optimal group is always a contiguous stretch, since including a smaller value never hurts and skipping a value between two chosen ones only wastes potential.

Observation 3: This turns the problem into: sort the array, then find the longest contiguous stretch whose "raise everyone up to the stretch's maximum" cost is at most k.

Observation 4: The cost of a window [left, right] in the sorted array is nums[right] * windowSize - sum(window), computable in O(1) using a running window sum, letting a variable-size sliding window solve this in one pass.

Recognizing that increment-only operations always favor raising to the group's own maximum is the key step that turns this into a sortable, windowable problem.
This is a sort-then-slide pattern: sorting exposes the structure, and a variable-size sliding window with an O(1) cost formula finds the answer in one linear pass over the sorted array.
6. Brute Force Solution
After sorting, for every right endpoint, extend left as far as possible while the cost of raising the window up to nums[right] stays within budget.
Step by step algorithm

items: Sort nums so equal-after-raising groups become contiguous stretches.
For every right endpoint, walk left backward from right, computing the raise-cost of the current window directly from its sum, stopping the moment the cost exceeds k.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting happens once upfront, since every subsequent cost calculation assumes a sorted array.
The cost is recomputed directly from a fresh running sum for each right endpoint, rather than reused across endpoints.
The inner walk stops the moment cost exceeds k, since extending further left from this same right endpoint would only cost more, never less.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every right endpoint is checked directly against every possible left endpoint, so the correct maximum group size is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for the sort, plus O(n squared) for the nested cost recomputation in the worst case.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sort.

Limitation: recomputing the window sum from scratch for every (left, right) pair ignores that a single running sum, adjusted incrementally as the window grows and shrinks, can answer the same question in one linear pass after sorting.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force recomputes the window sum from scratch for every candidate window. Instead, maintain a single running sum as right advances, adding nums[right] to it. Whenever the cost formula (nums[right] * windowSize - windowSum) exceeds k, shrink from the left, subtracting nums[left] from the running sum, until the cost is back within budget. Since left only ever moves forward and never resets, the entire pass after sorting runs in linear time.

Maintain a window with a left and right boundary over the sorted array, along with a running sum of its contents. Grow the window by advancing right and adding nums[right] to the sum. Whenever the cost of raising the window up to nums[right] exceeds k, shrink from the left, subtracting from the sum, until the cost is within budget. Track the maximum window length seen throughout.
9. Optimized Solution
Sort first, then grow the window from the right, shrinking from the left only when the raise-cost exceeds k.
Dry run for nums = [1, 4, 8, 13] (already sorted), k = 5

blocks.content: {"headers":["right","Value","windowSum","left","Cost = value * size - sum","Action","Best so far"],"rows":[["0","1","1","0","1*1 - 1 = 0","Fits (0 <= 5), window grows to [0,0]","1"],["1","4","5","0","4*2 - 5 = 3","Fits (3 <= 5), window grows to [0,1]","2"],["2","8","13","0 -> 1","8*3 - 13 = 11 exceeds k=5; shrink (remove index 0, sum becomes 12); recheck 8*2 - 12 = 4, fits","Shrunk to [1,2]","2"],["3","13","25","1 -> 2","13*3 - 25 = 14 exceeds k=5; shrink (remove index 1, sum becomes 21); recheck 13*2 - 21 = 5, fits","Shrunk to [2,3]","2"]]}

codes.python:
def max_frequency(nums, k):
    nums.sort()                                                              # equal values must sit together, so the window can only be a sorted stretch
    left = 0
    window_sum = 0
    best = 1
    for right in range(len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[right]
        while nums[right] * (right - left + 1) - window_sum > k:
            window_sum -= nums[left]                                        # too costly to raise everyone up to nums[right], shrink from the left
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_frequency([1, 4, 8, 13], 5))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for the sort, plus O(n) for the single sliding window pass.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sort (O(log n) to O(n) if the sort itself isn't in-place, depending on language).
Why This Works

After sorting, nums[right] is always the largest value in any window ending at right, so the cost to make the whole window equal to it is exactly nums[right] times the window size, minus whatever sum is already present. Whenever this exceeds k, the window is too expensive, and shrinking from the left (the cheapest members to drop, since they contribute least toward matching the target) is the correct way to reduce cost.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Cost of raising window to nums[right] is at most k","Keep growing the window by advancing right"],["Cost exceeds k","Shrink from the left until the cost is at most k again"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: windowSum is updated every time an element enters (on growth) or leaves (on shrink) the window, always reflecting its current total.
The shrink is a while loop, since more than one element might need to be removed from the left before the cost drops back within budget.
best is updated after any needed shrinking, always reflecting a currently-affordable window's true size.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem hinges on recognizing that increment-only operations always favor raising a group up to its own maximum, which turns an apparently combinatorial question into a sort-then-slide sliding window.
Common mistakes

items: Trying to raise a chosen group up to some value other than its own maximum, which is never cheaper under increment-only operations.
Forgetting to sort first, without which equal-after-raising groups are not guaranteed to be contiguous.
Recomputing the window sum from scratch on every step instead of maintaining it incrementally, which reintroduces the brute force's quadratic cost.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["nums has only 1 element","The answer is always 1, since a single element already has frequency 1"],["k = 0","The answer is the frequency of the most common existing value, since no operations can be spent at all"],["k is large enough to equalize the whole array","The answer is nums.length"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State explicitly why raising to the group's own maximum (rather than any other target) is always optimal under increment-only operations, since this justification is the crux of the problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Only increment operations, limited total budget, maximize how many elements can be made equal" points toward sorting first, then a variable-size sliding window with an O(1) cost formula based on a running sum.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if decrements were also allowed at the same cost? The optimal target would generally become the group's median rather than its maximum, changing the cost formula entirely.

How would you find the actual value that ends up with the highest frequency, not just the count? Track nums[right] at the moment best is updated, since that's the value the winning window gets raised to.

What if each operation had a different cost depending on which element it's applied to? The uniform running-sum cost formula would no longer hold, and a more general weighted approach would be needed.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A sort-then-slide variant of the variable-size sliding window family, alongside Minimum Size Subarray Sum and Max Consecutive Ones III, but requiring a sort as a setup step since the "window" here is over sorted values, not original array order.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (sort + variable-size sliding window): O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sort first, then a variable-size sliding window with an O(1) running-sum cost formula
Core Idea: Raising a group up to its own largest member is always the cheapest way to equalize it under increment-only operations
Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sort
Most Important Observation: Increment-only operations mean the optimal target for any group is always that group's own maximum value
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Sort, then slide a window whose "raise to the max" cost stays within budget
